patient_information: A 62-year-old male Thai police sergeant major from Kalasin Province, Thailand. His past medical history was notable for a liver fluke infection treated with praziquantel 10 years prior to presentation. Hepatitis B serology suggested a previous, resolved infection.
chief_complaint: An incidentally discovered solitary liver mass found on abdominal ultrasonography during an annual physical check-up.
history_of_present_illness: The patient was asymptomatic at the time of presentation for his annual physical. He denied any clinical symptoms, including weight loss, jaundice, or other gastrointestinal symptoms. A solitary mass was found in the liver on abdominal ultrasonography, and he was referred for further investigation.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from Kalasin Province in northeast Thailand, a region where the liver fluke, Opisthorchis viverrini, is endemic. An important risk factor is the local tradition of eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish, which frequently contains metacercariae of the fluke. The patient had a confirmed history of liver fluke infection treated a decade ago, and re-infection is common in the region.
physical_exam: The patient appeared in good health. Physical examination showed no jaundice, and the liver and spleen were not palpable. There were no liver stigmata or lymphadenopathy detected.
labs_and_diagnostics: Laboratory results showed normal liver function tests (AST, ALT, ALP, bilirubin). Hepatitis B serology was consistent with past infection (HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs positive, Anti-HBc positive), and Anti-HCV was negative. Tumor markers were significant for a markedly elevated CA19-9 of 342.80 U/mL, while AFP and CEA were within normal limits. Abdominal MRI revealed a single solid liver mass in segments VI/VII of the right liver lobe without marked bile duct dilatation. Post-surgical pathology of the 9x9 cm mass confirmed infiltrative compact glandular structures lined by dysplastic columnar cells with necrosis. Additionally, liver flukes (O. viverrini) were found in the adjacent bile duct.
differential_diagnosis: The primary differential diagnoses for the liver mass included hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), a metastatic tumor, and infections such as tuberculosis. Given the patient was asymptomatic with a high serum CA19-9 level and no history of chronic viral hepatitis, CCA was considered the most likely diagnosis.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was admitted to the hospital and underwent a hemihepatectomy. A large, 9 x 9 cm whitish-yellowish tumor was resected from the right liver lobe. Postoperatively, the patient was started on chemotherapy.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (CCA). This was confirmed by histology of the resected liver mass. The cancer is strongly associated with the patient's chronic liver fluke infection, evidenced by the presence of Opisthorchis viverrini flukes in the adjacent bile duct found during surgery. Key supporting evidence included the patient's epidemiological risk from living in northeast Thailand with a history of eating raw freshwater fish, and a markedly elevated CA19-9 tumor marker.
